question: How would you implement a thread-safe, in-memory rate limiter supporting millions of distinct users with dynamic rate limits, optimizing for minimal memory overhead and low lock contention?
context_or_scenario: You are designing an edge enforcement middleware for an internal Google Cloud microservice that receives high-throughput HTTP traffic (hundreds of thousands of QPS). Each authenticated user has a tier-dependent maximum burst capacity and refill rate (tokens per second). Naive implementations utilizing global mutexes or continuous background polling threads to update token balances fail under scale and exhaust resources.
rubric_points: Algorithm selection: Uses a Token Bucket or Sliding Window Counter utilizing a lazy timestamp-based refill mechanism (calculating token replenishment on demand using elapsed time rather than active background threads).

Concurrency control: Minimizes lock contention by avoiding a single global lock, instead using fine-grained striped locks, atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) operations, or concurrent hash maps partitioned by user ID.

Memory footprint and cleanup: Keeps the per-user state minimal (e.g., storing only a 64-bit timestamp and a floating-point/integer token count) and includes an explicit eviction strategy (such as TTL-based pruning or LRU cache) to reclaim memory from inactive users.

Edge-case handling: Accounts for system clock skew/monotonic time guarantees, integer overflow, handling bursts gracefully, and discusses trade-offs of single-node local caching versus distributed consistency.
